questions.q: What four sections does each ADR in this lesson contain?
options: Context, Options considered, Decision, Consequences
Summary, Budget, Timeline, Owner
Problem, Root Cause, Fix, Postmortem
Title, Author, Date, Signature
questions.explain: That four-part structure, from Lesson 22, is what makes an ADR a record of reasoning rather than just a statement of what was decided.

questions.q: Why does ADR-001 explicitly write down that 'the hub becomes a dependency every spoke relies on' as a consequence, rather than only listing benefits?
options: Azure requires every ADR to list exactly one negative consequence
A real ADR records the honest cost of a decision, not just its upside -- and this specific cost becomes directly relevant to ADR-003
It is a placeholder sentence with no further relevance later in the lesson
Because hub-and-spoke was ultimately rejected in favor of a flat network
questions.explain: Writing the uncomfortable consequence down is what makes ADR-003's existence make sense -- the gap it closes was named as a tradeoff from the start.

questions.q: Why is the shared hub services' RTO/RPO target in ADR-003 set to match Customer Portal's tightest target rather than an average across all three product teams?
options: Customer Portal pays for a higher service tier than the other teams
A shared dependency can never recover slower than the fastest tier counting on it, or that tier's own target becomes meaningless
Averages are not permitted in Azure DR planning
Fleet Analytics' target was used instead, since it is the loosest
questions.explain: If the hub recovered on Fleet Analytics' 24-hour timeline, Customer Portal's 1-hour target would be meaningless, since the hub is what Customer Portal's own failover depends on.

questions.q: What does the quarterly DR game day's Step 2 specifically validate that Step 1 does not?
options: That the billing invoice for the secondary region is correct
That Customer Portal's database contains the expected number of rows
That the hub's own failover works -- that spokes in the secondary region can still reach the internet and resolve internal DNS
That the primary region's firewall logs were archived correctly
questions.explain: Step 1 only proves the application tier failed over; Step 2 proves the shared network layer the application depends on actually works in the secondary region too.

questions.q: Why did Harlow Creek choose an active-passive DR pattern over active-active for most tiers?
options: Active-active is not supported by Azure Firewall
Active-passive is required for any tier with an RPO under one hour
The cost of running every tier live in two regions simultaneously isn't justified given Fleet Analytics' and Dispatch's actual RTO targets
Active-passive was the only option considered
questions.explain: Active-passive was deliberately chosen based on a documented cost-versus-recovery-speed tradeoff, following the comparison Lesson 15 taught -- not because no alternative was ever considered.
